title: Psalm 39: A Breath and a Sojourner
summary: A man determined to keep silent in front of the wicked finds that his silence only feeds his sorrow, until he breaks it with a prayer. He asks God to show him how short his life is, confesses that every human being is only a breath, places his hope in God, asks for deliverance from his sins, and ends by begging God to look away so he can know some cheer before he dies.
story: Psalm 38 ended with a cry for help from a man under God's discipline. Psalm 39 continues in that register but turns to a wider question: the brevity of human life. It is one of the most searching laments in the Psalter and one of the few that end without resolution. It reads almost like a psalm version of Ecclesiastes, sharing that book's key word for life as breath or vapor. Its closing request, that God look away, is startling, and it gives the church words for the times when faith and despair sit side by side.
historical:
The heading names the choirmaster and Jeduthun, and attributes the psalm to David. Jeduthun was a Levitical musician appointed by David, with Heman and Asaph, to lead music and thanksgiving before the LORD (1 Chronicles 16:41-42; 25:1-6). His name also appears in the headings of Psalms 62 and 77, and some scholars think it names a musical guild descended from him or a style of performance rather than the man himself. The Hebrew preposition can mean for Jeduthun, by Jeduthun, or after the manner of Jeduthun, and translations differ.

The psalm gives no specific historical setting. Verse 1 suggests the speaker was among the wicked, perhaps accused or mocked, and chose not to answer them. Verse 10 speaks of God's scourge, which suggests illness or some affliction he understood as discipline. Scholars differ on whether it was written by David or later placed in a collection associated with him.
cultural:
Verse 5 measures a lifetime in handbreadths, the width of a hand across four fingers, one of the smallest units of length in the ancient world. The image of the moth in verse 11 reflects the way moths destroyed woolen clothing, a household's portable wealth. What a person holds dear is eaten away quietly. Heaping up riches without knowing who will gather them echoes a concern also voiced in Ecclesiastes 2:18-21.

The word pair foreigner and stranger in verse 12 describes resident aliens, people who lived in Israel without owning land and depended on the goodwill of their hosts. Israel's law commanded care for such people (Leviticus 19:34) and reminded Israel that it too had been a stranger in Egypt. God said the land itself was his, and that the Israelites were strangers and sojourners with him (Leviticus 25:23). David used the same language when he prayed before the people about the offerings for the temple (1 Chronicles 29:15). To call oneself a sojourner with God was to confess that life and land were on loan.
literary: The psalm moves from silence to speech. Verses 1 to 3 describe a vow of silence that becomes unbearable, until the fire burned and the psalmist spoke. Verses 4 to 13 are the prayer itself, framed as one long quotation. The Selah after verses 5 and 11 marks two parallel statements of the same truth: every human being is a breath. Between them come hope (verse 7) and a plea for deliverance from sin (verse 8), then a return to silence (verse 9) that is now a silence before God rather than before the wicked. The ending is abrupt and unresolved: before I depart and am no more. The psalm's refusal to tie up its ending is part of its honesty.

outline.t: A vow of silence that cannot hold
Teach me my end: every man is a breath
My hope is in You: deliverance from sin and discipline
A stranger with God: hear, and look away

doctrines.note: Human life is fleeting, measured in handbreadths, a breath and a vapor. The psalm doesn't treat this as a reason for despair alone but as the truth a person needs to know in order to hope rightly.
In the middle of the psalm's bleakness comes verse 7: My hope is in You. Hope here is not optimism about circumstances but a choice to look to God when everything else is breath.
The psalm gives voice to suffering that doesn't resolve in the text. It shows that faith can include days when the most one can ask is a little relief before the end.

words.note: Hevel, breath or vapor. It is the key word of Ecclesiastes, often translated vanity or meaningless. It appears in verses 5, 6, and 11. The image is of something real but fleeting, like breath on a cold morning. The psalm uses it not to call life worthless but to call it brief and unable to bear the weight of ultimate trust.

Tselem, image. In Genesis 1:27 it describes humanity made in God's image. In verse 6 the BSB renders it phantom, a shadow or mere image. The same word that names human dignity can describe a person as insubstantial. Both are true of us: made in God's image, yet passing like a shadow.

Ger, sojourner or resident alien. It names someone who lives in a land not his own, without an inheritance there. In verse 12 the psalmist says he is a foreigner dwelling with God, like all his fathers, recalling Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who lived in Canaan as strangers. To be a ger with God is to depend on him as host.

christ: The psalm asks what hope a fleeting human life can have. The New Testament answers by pointing to Christ, who shared that brief life, died, and was raised, so that those who belong to him will not simply vanish like breath. Hebrews 11:13 describes the patriarchs as strangers and exiles on the earth who were looking for a better country, and 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians sojourners and exiles. Both texts draw on the same language as verse 12. The link is thematic: the psalm's ache over mortality and its sense of being a guest on earth find their answer in the resurrection and the promise of a lasting home. Christians can pray this psalm honestly because they share its frailty, and hopefully because they know the one who has overcome death.

hard.q: Why does the psalmist ask God to look away from him?
hard.a: Verse 13 is one of the strangest requests in the Psalms: Turn Your gaze away from me. Most of the Psalter begs God to look, see, and turn his face toward the sufferer. Here the psalmist feels God's gaze as discipline (verses 10 and 11) and asks for a reprieve. Job makes a similar plea (Job 7:19; 10:20-21). Interpreters generally read the request as the cry of someone overwhelmed by God's correcting hand, not a rejection of God himself; the same prayer asks God to hear and not be deaf to his tears. Some find in it a model of radical honesty: Scripture allows a believer to say that God's nearness feels unbearable. Others note that the psalm's bleak ending is balanced by the rest of the Psalter, which moves toward praise. The psalm doesn't resolve the tension, and readers are free to let it stand as it is. Readers who find in verse 13 their own wish to be gone should not carry it alone, any more than the psalmist did: he said it to God, and it is right to say it to a trusted friend, a pastor, or a doctor as well, or in a crisis to a local crisis line or emergency service (in the United States, call or text 988).

questions: The psalmist asks God to show him how fleeting his life is. How might knowing that change the way you spend your days?
What have you been heaping up (money, reputation, achievements) without knowing who will gather it?
Have you ever felt that God's attention was more than you could bear? What would it mean to bring even that feeling to him in prayer?
